listeningParts.title: Booking a guided city tour
listeningParts.contextDescription: A tourist phones a tour company to book a walking tour.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, City Walks, this is Maria. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Hello. I'd like to book a walking tour for this weekend, please. I'm visiting with my family.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Wonderful. We have three tours at the weekend. The History Walk, the Food Tour and the Night Walk. Which one interests you?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: What's the difference between them?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The History Walk visits the old town, the cathedral and the castle. It takes about two hours. The Food Tour goes to the market and five small restaurants where you can taste local dishes. That one lasts three hours. And the Night Walk is about ghosts and old stories. It starts at nine o'clock in the evening.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: My children are eight and ten, so I don't think the Night Walk is a good idea. They'd be too tired, and maybe scared.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That's true. Children under twelve aren't allowed on the Night Walk anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: I think the History Walk sounds best. My son loves castles.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great choice. On Saturday it starts at ten in the morning, and on Sunday at eleven.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Saturday morning, please. On Sunday we're taking the train to the coast.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem. How many people?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Two adults and two children.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Adult tickets are eighteen dollars and children's tickets are nine dollars. But we have a family ticket for two adults and two children, which costs forty-five dollars. That saves you nine dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Perfect, the family ticket then.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: And can I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Helen Bradshaw. B-R-A-D-S-H-A-W.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a mobile number, in case we need to contact you?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks. So, the tour starts outside the main entrance of the Central Library. Do you know where that is?

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Is that near the train station?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Not exactly. It's in Market Square, opposite the big fountain. Look for a guide holding a yellow umbrella. That's how you'll find us.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: A yellow umbrella. Okay. What should we bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Comfortable shoes, because the streets in the old town are very uneven. And bring some water. There's a short break in the middle of the tour at a café near the castle, if anyone wants to buy a snack.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: What happens if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The tour goes ahead in the rain, so bring a coat. Only if the weather is really dangerous, for example in a storm, do we cancel, and then you get your money back.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: And is the tour suitable for children?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, very. The guide gives every child a small activity book with questions to answer during the tour. They usually love it.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: That sounds great. How do I pay?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: You can pay now by card, and I'll email you a booking reference. Just show it to the guide on Saturday, on your phone or on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Lovely. Can we go inside the castle during the tour?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The tour stops outside the castle, and the guide tells you its history. If you want to go inside, you need a separate ticket, but you get ten per cent off if you show your tour booking.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Brilliant. One more question. Is the tour in English only?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The Saturday morning tour is in English, but we also have tours in Spanish and French on other days. And the guide speaks slowly and clearly, so it's easy to follow, even for children.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Good. And how many people are usually in a group?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We never have more than twenty people, so everyone can hear the guide and ask questions. Saturday is usually quite busy, though, so I'm glad you're booking now. There are only six places left.

dialogue.speaker: Tourist
dialogue.text: Then I'm glad I called today. Thank you very much, Maria.

listeningParts.title: Welcome to the summer arts festival
listeningParts.contextDescription: A festival organiser speaks on local radio about this year's summer arts festival.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, and thank you for inviting me. I'm Paul Grant, the director of the Riverside Summer Festival, and I'm delighted to tell your listeners about this year's programme. The festival runs for ten days, from Friday the eighteenth of July to Sunday the twenty-seventh, and this is our twentieth year, so we've planned something special.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The festival has always been about bringing all kinds of art to everyone in the town, and that's still our aim. This year we have more than a hundred and fifty events, including music, theatre, dance, comedy and film, and about a third of them are completely free.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about some of the highlights. The opening concert on the first Friday will take place in Riverside Park. It's free, and we're expecting around five thousand people, so do come early. The music starts at seven, but the gates open at five, and there'll be food stalls selling dishes from around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For theatre lovers, the main event is a new play written by a local writer, Anna Price, about the history of the town's old factory. It will be performed in the Old Mill, which was once part of that factory, so the setting is perfect. Tickets are twelve pounds, and there are eight performances.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Families are very important to us. Every day there will be activities for children in the Library Gardens, including storytelling, face painting and music workshops. These are all free, and you don't need to book. On the middle Saturday, we also have a children's parade, and children are invited to make costumes at workshops during the first week of the festival.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: This year, for the first time, we're also holding an outdoor film festival. Every evening at nine thirty, we'll show a film on a big screen by the river. Bring a blanket or a chair. The films are free, but there are only five hundred places, so you need to get a ticket from the box office first.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: For people who want to try something themselves, there are lots of workshops. You can learn to paint, to make pottery or to dance the tango. Most workshops cost five pounds, and all the money goes to help young artists in the town.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: And for comedy fans, there are comedy nights every Friday and Saturday in the back room of the Swan Hotel. Some of the comedians are famous, and some are performing for the very first time. These shows are only for adults, and tickets cost eight pounds. Last year they sold out very quickly, so please book early.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Some practical information now. The festival box office is in the Town Hall, and it's open from nine until six every day. You can also buy tickets online on our website, which is the easiest way, especially for popular events. Many events are in the town centre, so we suggest leaving your car at home. There will be extra buses in the evenings, and the last bus leaves the town centre at midnight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We also need help! Every year we rely on around two hundred volunteers. They do all kinds of jobs, from selling programmes to helping artists. Volunteers get a festival T-shirt and free tickets to two events of their choice. If you're interested, please come to a meeting on Monday the seventh of July at the Town Hall.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Finally, the closing event. On the last night, there will be a fireworks display over the river at ten o'clock. It's the biggest fireworks display in the region and it's completely free. We hope to see you all there.

listeningParts.title: Choosing a topic for a tourism project
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two tourism students, Sam and Lina, discuss ideas for a group project.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Hi Lina. So, we need to choose a topic for our tourism project by Friday. Have you had any ideas?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: A few. I was thinking about ecotourism, you know, holidays that try to protect the environment. It's very popular at the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: It is, but I think lots of other groups will choose it. Our lecturer said she's already read about twenty projects on ecotourism. We might find it hard to say something new.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: That's a good point. What about you? Any ideas?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: I was thinking about tourism in our own town. Lots of people visit the castle and the old town in summer, but almost nobody comes in winter. We could look at how the town could attract visitors all year.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. And it's local, so we can do our own research. We could talk to people who work in hotels and shops.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. And the tourist information office might give us some numbers on visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Okay, let's choose that. How should we collect information? I think a questionnaire for tourists would be good.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: In winter there won't be many tourists to ask, though. Maybe we should interview people in local businesses instead. Hotel managers would know a lot about the busy and quiet seasons.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: True. But a questionnaire could still work if we put it online. We could ask people who visited last summer why they didn't come in winter.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Okay, let's do both, then. I'll organise the interviews, because I know the manager of the Castle Hotel. My aunt works there.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Great. And I'll write the questionnaire. I did one last term for another course, so I know how to make it short and clear.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: What about examples from other places? It would be good to see what other towns have done.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Yes. I read about a town in Austria that started a winter food festival. Now it's one of their busiest times of year. That could be a good case study.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: And there's that town in Scotland that has a winter light festival, where they light up old buildings at night. It's a bit like our castle.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Oh, I've seen photos of that. It looks beautiful. Do you think our town could do something similar?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Maybe. The castle would look amazing with lights on it. But we'd need to find out how much it would cost, and who would pay. That could be a question for our interviews.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Good idea. We could ask the hotel managers if they'd be willing to help pay for an event that brings more visitors in winter. After all, they would get more customers.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Exactly. Let's write that down so we don't forget it. And we could also ask the people at the tourist information office what they think about the idea, because they talk to visitors every day.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Perfect. Two case studies should be enough. Now, how long does the report need to be?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Three thousand words, plus a ten-minute presentation to the class.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: When's the deadline?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: The report is due on the fifteenth of December, and the presentations are the week after.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: That doesn't give us much time. We should start the interviews next week.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Agreed. Shall we meet every Wednesday to check our progress?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Wednesday is difficult for me, I have a long lecture in the afternoon. Can we do Thursday?

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Thursday's fine. Let's say Thursdays at twelve, in the library café.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.text: Okay. And one more thing. Let's share all our documents online so we can both edit them. That way we won't lose anything.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.text: Good idea. I'll set it up tonight and send you the link.

listeningParts.title: The history of the bicycle
listeningParts.contextDescription: A talk at a transport museum about how the bicycle developed.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'm going to tell you the story of one of the simplest and most useful machines ever invented: the bicycle. There are more than a billion bicycles in the world today, but the bicycle as we know it is only about a hundred and forty years old.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The first machine that looked something like a bicycle was invented in Germany in 1817 by a man called Karl Drais. It had two wheels and a wooden frame, but no pedals. The rider sat on the seat and pushed along the ground with his feet, a bit like a child's balance bike today. People called it a running machine. One reason Drais was interested in it was that, at the time, horses were very expensive to feed after a series of bad harvests.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The next important step came in France in the 1860s, when pedals were added to the front wheel. These machines were popular, but they were very uncomfortable. The wheels were made of wood with iron around the outside, and on the stone roads of the time, the ride was extremely bumpy. In fact, people gave them the nickname 'boneshakers'.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1870s, a new design appeared that you've probably seen in old photographs: the penny-farthing. It had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. Why such a big wheel? Because the pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, a bigger wheel meant the bicycle travelled further with each turn of the pedals, so riders could go faster. But it was also dangerous. The rider sat very high up, and if the wheel hit a stone, he could easily fall forward over the handlebars. Penny-farthings were mostly ridden by young men who enjoyed the excitement.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The real breakthrough came in 1885, when an Englishman, John Kemp Starley, produced what he called the 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Because of the chain, the wheels didn't need to be large, so the rider sat closer to the ground. It was much safer and easier to ride, and its basic shape is the same as almost every bicycle today.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: A few years later, another important invention made cycling much more comfortable: the air-filled rubber tyre. It was developed by John Dunlop, a vet in Belfast, who wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable to ride. Air-filled tyres made the ride smoother and faster, and soon all bicycles had them.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the 1890s, there was a bicycle boom. For the first time, ordinary people could travel easily beyond their own town or village, and cycling clubs became very popular. The bicycle was particularly important for women. It gave them a new kind of freedom to travel on their own, and it even changed fashion, because long, heavy skirts were difficult to ride in, so women began to wear shorter skirts and looser clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, the car became more popular in many countries, and cycling declined. But today, the bicycle is having a comeback. Many cities are building cycle lanes, and electric bicycles are making cycling possible for older people and in hilly places. In the Netherlands, there are actually more bicycles than people, and around a quarter of all journeys are made by bike. Cycling is also very good for your health, and it doesn't cause pollution, which is why many governments now want to encourage it.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Now, if you'd like to follow me into the next room, you can see some of these early bicycles for yourselves, including a real boneshaker. And if you're brave, you can even try sitting on our penny-farthing.

readingPassages.title: The world's first public museums
paragraphs: Today, museums are among the most popular places to visit anywhere in the world. Every year, millions of people visit famous museums such as the Louvre in Paris or the British Museum in London, and almost every town has a museum of some kind. But the idea of a public museum, open to everyone, is surprisingly recent. For most of history, collections of art and interesting objects belonged to rich and powerful people, and only their friends and important visitors were allowed to see them.

In Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, wealthy people often created what were called 'cabinets of curiosities'. These were rooms filled with all kinds of unusual objects: shells, rocks, stuffed animals, ancient coins, scientific instruments and works of art. There was often little order to these collections. A crocodile might hang from the ceiling above a painting, with a piece of coral next to a clock. Some objects were not even real: collectors sometimes paid large sums for the horns of unicorns, which were in fact the long teeth of a sea animal called the narwhal. Although these collections were not very scientific, they encouraged an interest in the natural world, and some of them later became the basis of important museums. The aim was to amaze visitors and to show how rich and well-travelled the owner was.

One of the first museums to open its doors to the public was the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, England, which opened in 1683. It was based on the collection of a man called Elias Ashmole, who gave his objects to the University of Oxford. Visitors had to pay to enter, and at first the museum was mainly used by students and scholars. The building also contained a laboratory where scientists carried out chemical experiments, so the museum was a place for research as well as for looking at objects. However, it was an important step, because the collection now belonged to an institution rather than a private person.

The British Museum, which opened in 1759, was one of the first national museums. It was created after a doctor and collector, Sir Hans Sloane, left his huge collection of more than seventy thousand objects to the nation when he died. Entry was free, but it was not easy to get in. Visitors had to apply in writing for a ticket, and they were taken round in small groups by a guide who often hurried them through the rooms. In the early years, only about ten thousand people visited each year.

The French Revolution changed the idea of the museum. In 1793, the revolutionary government opened the Louvre, which had been a royal palace, as a public museum. The paintings and sculptures that had belonged to the king now belonged to the people, and the museum was open to everyone, free of charge, on certain days of the week. Ordinary working people could now see great works of art for the first time. Artists were also allowed in on special days to study and copy the paintings, which helped to train a new generation of painters. Many other countries followed this example in the nineteenth century.

During the nineteenth century, museums also began to organise their collections more carefully. Instead of mixing everything together like the old cabinets of curiosities, they divided objects into groups, such as natural history, archaeology and art, and arranged them in a logical order, often with written labels. Museums were seen as places where people could learn, and governments hoped they would help educate the working classes. Some museums even opened in the evening, so that people could visit after work.

Today, museums continue to change. Many now use digital technology, such as touch screens, audio guides on visitors' phones and virtual reality, and some allow people to explore their collections online from home. There are also important debates about who should own certain objects. Some objects in European museums were taken from other countries during periods of war or colonial rule, and those countries have asked for them to be returned. How museums respond to these requests is likely to be one of the biggest questions they face in the coming years.

readingPassages.title: Why we love to travel
paragraphs: Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world. Before the pandemic in 2020, there were around one and a half billion international trips every year, and tourism provided jobs for about one in ten workers worldwide. But why do people travel? It is not always for the reasons we might expect. Researchers who study tourism have found that people's motivations are often more complicated than simply wanting to relax or see famous places.

One of the best-known explanations was developed by the tourism researcher Graham Dann in the 1970s. Dann suggested that travel is influenced by two kinds of factors, which he called 'push' and 'pull' factors. Push factors are the reasons people want to leave home, such as stress at work, boredom or the desire for adventure. Pull factors are the things that attract people to a particular place, such as beaches, history, good weather or famous food. In other words, push factors explain why people want to travel, and pull factors explain where they choose to go.

Another researcher, Philip Pearce, argued that people's reasons for travelling change as they gain more experience. He described this as a 'travel career'. According to Pearce, inexperienced travellers often want comfort, safety and relaxation. As people travel more, they become more interested in learning about other cultures, meeting local people and developing themselves. Not all researchers agree with this idea, but many tourism companies use it when they design holidays for different groups of customers. For example, a company might offer simple beach holidays with everything included for first-time travellers, and more adventurous trips, such as staying with local families or volunteering on a farm, for people who have travelled widely. Some travellers, of course, never follow this pattern and are happy to return to the same beach hotel every year.

In recent years, a new kind of motivation has become important: the wish to share experiences on social media. A survey of young British travellers found that about forty per cent chose their holiday destination partly because it would look good in photos online. Some places have become extremely popular because of photographs shared on the internet. A quiet lake, a colourful street or a small café can suddenly attract thousands of visitors after a famous person posts a picture of it. Local businesses may be happy at first, but the sudden crowds can be difficult to manage. This has brought money to some small towns, but it has also caused problems, as huge numbers of visitors arrive at places that are not prepared for them.

This problem, known as overtourism, is now a serious concern in many popular destinations. In Venice, for example, the number of tourists is far greater than the number of people who live there, and many local residents have moved away because of high rents and crowded streets. In Barcelona, which receives tens of millions of visitors a year, some residents have protested against tourists, and the city has limited the building of new hotels in the centre. Some popular natural places, such as beaches and mountains, have also been damaged by too many visitors.

Cities and countries are trying different ways to manage this problem. Some, like Venice, now charge an entry fee to day visitors at busy times. Others encourage tourists to visit at less busy times of the year, or to explore less famous areas. Amsterdam has stopped advertising itself to certain types of visitors, such as large groups who come mainly for parties. Bhutan, a small country in the Himalayas, has long followed a policy of 'high value, low impact' tourism, charging visitors a daily fee that is used to protect the environment and culture.

Tourism therefore brings both benefits and costs. It can create jobs, protect historic buildings and help people understand other cultures. But it can also damage the environment and make life difficult for local people. Many experts believe the solution is 'sustainable tourism', which means travelling in a way that respects local people and nature, and makes sure that the money from tourism helps the communities that receive visitors. As more people around the world are able to travel, finding this balance will become even more important.

readingPassages.title: Learning to play: the benefits of music lessons
paragraphs: Many parents send their children to music lessons, hoping that learning to play an instrument will help them do better at school. It is often said that music makes children cleverer, and there are many books and websites that claim music lessons improve memory, concentration and even mathematics. But what does the research actually show? The answer is more complicated, and in some ways more interesting, than these popular claims suggest.

The idea that music can make people more intelligent became very popular in the 1990s after a small study suggested that listening to music by Mozart for ten minutes improved students' performance on a test of spatial skills. Newspapers reported the result as the 'Mozart effect', and some parents began playing classical music to their babies. However, later studies found that the effect was very small and lasted only a few minutes. Listening to any music that people enjoyed seemed to have a similar effect, probably because it made them feel more alert and in a better mood.

Learning to play an instrument is very different from simply listening. It requires many hours of practice, and it involves reading music, coordinating the hands, listening carefully and remembering long pieces. Because of this, many researchers expected that music lessons would improve other skills too. Some studies have found that children who take music lessons do better at school than children who do not. But this does not necessarily mean that the lessons cause the improvement.

The problem is that children who take music lessons are often different from other children in important ways. Their families may have more money, since lessons and instruments can be expensive. Their parents may be more interested in education. And the children themselves may be more patient or hardworking, which is why they continue with lessons in the first place. Any of these things could explain why they do better at school, even without the music. Researchers call this a problem of cause and effect. If two things happen together, it does not always mean that one causes the other. For example, children who eat breakfast may get better marks, but this might be because their families are more organised, not because of the breakfast itself. The same problem makes it difficult to know whether music lessons really make a difference.

To solve this problem, researchers need to carry out experiments in which children are chosen at random to receive music lessons or not. In one well-known study in Canada, six-year-old children were randomly given a year of keyboard lessons, singing lessons, drama lessons or no lessons. At the end of the year, the children who had music lessons showed a small improvement in IQ compared with the others. However, other experiments have found little or no effect, and a large review of many studies in 2017 concluded that music lessons have no clear effect on general intelligence or school results.

Does this mean music lessons are a waste of time? Not at all. Even if music does not make children cleverer in general, it has many other benefits. Learning an instrument can teach children, even very young ones, to set goals and work towards them, to deal with mistakes and to perform in front of other people. Playing in a band, orchestra or choir helps children to cooperate and make friends. And there is good evidence that music training improves children's ability to hear differences in sounds, which may help them learn languages. Many adults who stopped music lessons as children say they wish they had continued, and research suggests that playing music can be a source of enjoyment and relaxation throughout life, even in old age.

Perhaps the most important reason to learn music, however, is simply that music itself is truly valuable. For thousands of years, people in every culture in the world have sung, danced and played instruments together. Music can bring great pleasure and help people express their feelings. Many experts argue that we should not have to prove that music improves mathematics before we give children the chance to learn it. Instead, music should be part of every child's education because it is an important part of human life.
